title: "Discussion"
output: html_document
---

Our EDA provided important context for understanding our data, as it provided us with information related to both both green space availability and NYC community health. Cleaning and preparing the data required making two key decisions: choosing how to handle parks that span multiple community districts and choosing which variables to analyze. Regarding the first issue, acreage was not reported by community, so we divided each park’s area evenly across the districts it belonged to, allowing for a consistent measure of green space per capita. This approach enabled us to identify clear differences in green space distribution. Staten Island consistently had the highest acres of green space per capita, while Manhattan had the lowest. The distribution of park sizes also varied by borough, with Staten Island showing both the largest parks and the widest range of park sizes, whereas other boroughs, particularly Manhattan, proved to have smaller green spaces.

Regarding the second decision, we focused on analyzing variables that we though might be related as well as variables we thought to be the most objective measures of health. EDA of the community health data showed socioeconomic patterns that aligned with our expectations. Boroughs exhibited distinct racial and age compositions, and different health indicators showed strong correlations with socioeconomic measures. Higher levels of poverty, unemployment, and people who were uninsured were associated with lower physical activity and lower rates of on-time high school graduation. Although these relationships show correlation rather than causation, they provide a valuable foundation for understanding how green space accessibility might relate to health and social outcomes across NYC communities.
